toc.title: First, a quick recap of validation
Emotions come from a polyvagal state

blocks.p: Are you able to normalize your emotions? Do you know what normalization is? Fret not. Here I'll teach you what normalization is and how you can start normalizing yourself now. It helps you connect your cognitions with your present moment experience, which is really important not just for trauma recovery, but for emotional regulation in general.

Emotional normalization is basically just making sense of your emotions based on your life context. It's a cognitive self-regulation tool that you can use after emotional validation, and it can help to alleviate emotional dysregulation that you might be experiencing.

Normalization is one of my three top-down self-regulation openers: validation, normalization, and giving permission. The basic idea of a top-down self-regulation opener is that it's possible to shift your polyvagal state, your body's state, from the brain to the body.

Normalization is a pretty darn crucial step, in my opinion, in unlocking the potential for trauma recovery and self-regulation. But it shouldn't be seen as a standalone solution to move out of a traumatized state. It's the second of three top-down steps that create the grounds for opening up potential self-regulation.

blocks.h: First, a quick recap of validation

blocks.p: Normalization builds on validation, so let's do a really quick recap. Validation is confirming that what you are experiencing is true. It's an objective and truthful acceptance of what you actually feel emotionally. For example, admitting to yourself that you feel sad is validating of your emotional experience. Likewise, telling your feelings to somebody else and having them name your feelings as sad could also be validating.

After validating your emotions, the next step is to normalize them. Your emotions not only truly exist, they also have a reason for existing within you. They don't just come out of nowhere. In fact, I'd be willing to bet that if somebody else had similar life circumstances to you, they would likely feel the same way and be left with similar emotions, similar cognitions, similar impulses, and similar sensations as well. And yeah, probably a similar stuck state.

I see this all the time in my client work. I have personally yet to meet with a client that I thought had random feelings. I would say that 100% of my caseload over the years have had present-day emotions that stem from present-day experiences, past experiences, or both. Their emotions make sense based on the context of their present day and/or their earlier life.

If others had the same life context as you, they would likely end up with a similar stuck defensive state and experience similar emotions, like the ones that may have brought you here. So just like you would reassure somebody else in that situation that their feelings are normal, I invite you to do the same for yourself. Your emotions are normal and understandable given the circumstances you grew up in and/or that you are currently in. That is the essence of normalization.

I recommend that you focus on normalization, and not on retelling your trauma, unless you're in therapy and that's the path you're on. Unless you can handle it or you're doing it with a professional, I really don't recommend delving deeper into the life circumstances that led to your present-day dysregulation, at least not now.

The focus may need to be on acknowledging and accepting that your emotions are valid and normal. It's completely okay to keep the past general when it comes to your self-regulation or unstucking process, and still understand that your specific emotions make sense based on your life circumstances.

When it comes to normalizing your emotions, be specific and objective about the emotions you're working with. The basic idea is: these emotions are normal based on my life circumstances. It might sound like:

ul: "The emotion that brings me to trauma recovery is normal."
"My emotions make sense in this context."
"My emotions make sense based on my life context."

blocks.p: Pick what works for you, or make up your own. What would it sound like if you were to normalize your emotions based on your life circumstances?

blocks.h: Emotions come from a polyvagal state

blocks.p: You can probably guess that emotions come from a polyvagal state. Basically, emotions come from the state of our body, which can be more prepared for safety and connection, or for defense: running away, fighting, or shutting down.

Emotions are complex, so let's acknowledge that. But while they're complex and multi-layered, they ultimately stem from a polyvagal state, which is a biological process. This is not to diminish the significance of your valid felt experience of your emotions. It's to understand that they are a natural reaction to the context of your life.

Emotions are not inherently good or bad. They're a normal response to circumstances. Recognizing this can help to reduce the intensity of the feelings associated with difficult life circumstances. That's normalization.

In hindsight, it's easy to question why we didn't take certain actions, or why our parents didn't act differently. It may be more helpful to recognize that our bodies naturally adapt to defensive states in response to challenging circumstances, and it's not uncommon for us to get biologically stuck in these states. That's what trauma is.

This is a normal reaction. It falls within the range of expected and typical biological responses to situations that trigger a defensive autonomic state, like flight, fight, shutdown, or freeze. In fact, these biological shifts are what allow us to survive, not only us, but every organism before us. These normal shifts to safety and danger have been passed down through evolution and are encoded into our DNA.

Not only are our polyvagal shifts normal, they're necessary. And the emotions that come from a polyvagal state make a lot more sense when you look at them from the viewpoint of biology. Your neuroceptive shifts, your stuck polyvagal state, and your felt experience of that state all make sense, and are expected outcomes of your life context.

Normalization might not be easy, and I invite you to acknowledge that. [Polyvagal ladder](piece:autonomic-nervous-system) climbing is difficult, not just for you, but for all of us. That difficulty is normal, and an expected part of trauma recovery. All of this might be brand new for you. So just acknowledge, and maybe even accept, that this is not easy, and it doesn't have to be easy. We're going to take steps in the right direction, little by little.

Normalizing can help you to reduce shame and blame, and more. Let's bring it back to the top-down self-regulation openers: validation, normalization, and giving permission. If we can do those, it lowers the cognitions that get in the way of self-regulation.

Your body has to self-regulate. It is compelled to self-regulate, and it can do so. But trauma is the inability to self-regulate, or the difficulty with it. Your autonomic nervous system is stuck in a state of defense. But stuck means it's still trying to. It still has the impulse to self-regulate.

These top-down self-regulation openers help to align your cognitions with your stuck defensive state. They help clear out other cognitions, like blame, shame, or judgment, that keep you stuck. If you can validate your emotions as real and then normalize them based on the context of your life, the need for cognitions about shame, blame, and judgment probably goes down.

And if that goes down, your conscious mind, your cognitions at least, will be more in alignment with the present moment and with what's happening within you. If that's true, then the capacity for self-regulation to happen probably goes up. The next step builds on this: giving permission.
